		<item>
			<title>SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104012256.htm</link>
			<description>For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology.</description>
			<pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 05:43:44 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104012256.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104012254.htm</link>
			<description>NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.</description>
			<pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 06:22:33 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104012254.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104012248.htm</link>
			<description>MIT scientists have challenged two decades of conventional thinking by discovering that flexible molecular connections, rather than rigid ones, can unlock entirely new ways to arrange nanoparticles. The breakthrough could lead to a new generation of designer materials with unusual properties and applications in electronics, medicine, and energy.</description>
			<pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 07:23:36 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104012248.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104005226.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.</description>
			<pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 08:26:06 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104005226.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Goodbye, cavities? Scientists create gel that could regrow tooth enamel</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104005059.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have developed a revolutionary gel that could regrow lost tooth enamel by harnessing minerals naturally found in saliva, potentially overcoming one of dentistry’s biggest limitations. The regenerated enamel behaves much like healthy enamel, raising hopes for a simple treatment that could repair damaged teeth, prevent decay, and reduce sensitivity.</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 06:37:26 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104005059.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104004909.htm</link>
			<description>Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.</description>
			<pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 01:57:06 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104004909.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003207.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have developed a remarkable new membrane that separates crude oil at room temperature, using the oil itself to create microscopic filtration channels. The breakthrough could cut refining energy consumption by nearly 32%, carbon emissions by almost 38%, and operating costs by 36%, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industries.</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 09:04:07 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003207.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>A clever molecular trick unlocks previously impossible properties in glass</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003202.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have discovered how to reprogram the internal structure of glass using a special molecule that rearranges chemical bonds while lowering the melting temperature. The breakthrough could unlock entirely new glass materials with precisely controlled magnetic and optical properties, opening possibilities for advanced electronics, sensors, and other technologies.</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 08:36:51 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003202.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003157.htm</link>
			<description>A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting their biological clocks. Researchers found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise.</description>
			<pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 07:50:48 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003157.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003154.htm</link>
			<description>Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 04:46:21 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003154.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003152.htm</link>
			<description>NASA’s Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone nearly 50 years after its launch, even as engineers battle dwindling power and mysterious technical problems. A clever energy-saving maneuver has extended the spacecraft’s scientific mission, while an unexplained 48-hour communications blackout recently gave NASA a scare. On November 18, Voyager 1 will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, making even the simplest round-trip communication take 48 hours.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 03:11:10 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003152.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003149.htm</link>
			<description>Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 21:52:16 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003149.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003146.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.</description>
			<pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 08:24:52 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261103003146.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202845.htm</link>
			<description>A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 07:15:18 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202845.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202838.htm</link>
			<description>A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 07:51:53 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202838.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>400,000-year-old teeth reveal a stunning twist in human evolution</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202836.htm</link>
			<description>A groundbreaking discovery is rewriting the story of human evolution, revealing that an ancient human species once thought to be an evolutionary dead end may have left genetic traces in people alive today. By extracting proteins from 400,000-year-old Homo erectus teeth discovered in China, scientists uncovered evidence suggesting that these early humans interbred with Denisovans, another mysterious ancient human group. That genetic connection may have eventually reached modern populations in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, and other parts of Southeast Asia.</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 08:05:12 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202836.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202833.htm</link>
			<description>A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 08:03:02 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202833.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202831.htm</link>
			<description>Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.</description>
			<pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 22:47:09 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202831.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202829.htm</link>
			<description>A single gene-editing treatment could someday protect against heart disease, high cholesterol, and other common conditions for decades, potentially replacing lifelong medications. But scientists warn that permanently altering genes introduces risks that could take years to emerge, making long-term safety a critical challenge.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 23:30:57 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202829.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists turn viruses into weapons against deadly superbugs</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202828.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists are advancing a promising new way to fight antibiotic-resistant infections by using viruses that specifically target and kill harmful bacteria. An international team has released the first coordinated guidelines for personalized phage therapy, offering a roadmap for safely bringing this experimental treatment into clinical practice. Early findings are encouraging, with one study reporting improvement in 77% of patients and the disappearance of targeted bacteria in 61%.</description>
			<pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 21:40:33 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202828.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202824.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between inflammation during pregnancy, placental damage, and autism-like traits in male mice, while females appeared naturally protected. The discovery could help explain why autism is diagnosed more frequently in boys and reveal new opportunities for early intervention.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 07:41:49 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102202824.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102075903.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 05:58:24 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102075903.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102075806.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 23:11:58 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102075806.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102075553.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists are calling for a major rethink of how we manage high blood pressure, suggesting that eating more potassium could be just as important as cutting back on salt. A new report finds that combining increased potassium intake with reduced sodium consumption may offer greater benefits for blood pressure control than sodium reduction alone.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 08:10:42 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261102075553.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010559.htm</link>
			<description>A major 24-year study involving more than 8,200 adults suggests that excess body weight may accelerate brain aging, leading to faster declines in memory, concentration, and decision-making skills. The connection was particularly strong among people over 65, raising concerns about the long-term effects of obesity on brain health.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 08:55:28 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010559.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010556.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 07:50:34 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010556.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists solve 30-year-old mystery and discover a hidden defense against inflammation</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010554.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have solved a decades-old mystery and uncovered a hidden immune system defense that protects healthy cells from the very inflammation meant to fight infections. The surprising discovery could lead to new approaches for treating cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and other conditions involving excessive inflammation.</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 06:05:46 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010554.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010552.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 23:05:31 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010552.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010549.htm</link>
			<description>A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to greater increases in body fat and body mass index (BMI) one year later, suggesting that the brain's sensitivity to food cues may help explain why ultra-processed diets are associated with obesity.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 20:00:13 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010549.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>A tiny squeeze dramatically changes the magnetism of exotic materials</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010541.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have discovered that a simple mechanical squeeze can dramatically alter the magnetic properties and electrical behavior of exotic materials called altermagnets. The surprising breakthrough could open the door to faster, more energy-efficient electronics and new technologies for quantum computing.</description>
			<pubDate>Wed, 04 Nov 2026 07:37:52 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010541.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010538.htm</link>
			<description>NASA satellites have captured an eerie, skull-shaped formation on a remote Antarctic island, but its haunting appearance conceals a troubling warning about melting glaciers. Unusually warm winter temperatures have exposed large areas of dark ice, potentially accelerating future melting and gradually transforming the skull's ghostly features.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 04:50:36 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010538.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover breaks historic record after traveling 28 miles</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010536.htm</link>
			<description>NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a historic record by traveling 28.10 miles across Mars, farther than any vehicle has ever driven on another world. Armed with groundbreaking autonomous navigation technology and increasingly advanced driving capabilities, the rover is pushing the boundaries of robotic exploration.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 06:28:04 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010536.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010533.htm</link>
			<description>Mysterious particles called neutrinos constantly stream through our bodies, and scientists are now detecting incredibly powerful versions arriving from distant cosmic sources using a massive observatory buried in Antarctic ice. These elusive “ghost particles” could hold extraordinary clues about the Big Bang, extreme cosmic events, and some of the universe’s greatest mysteries.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 08:42:07 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010533.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010525.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have discovered a possible loophole in the laws that normally prevent black holes from splitting apart, suggesting that extremely fast-spinning black holes might divide into two. The surprising finding raises the possibility of an entirely new black hole phenomenon that future telescopes could potentially detect.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 20:27:49 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261101010525.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221215.htm</link>
			<description>Eating an avocado and a cup of mango every day may provide surprising benefits for heart health, according to a new study involving adults with prediabetes. After just eight weeks, participants experienced significant improvements in blood vessel function and diastolic blood pressure, particularly among men. These benefits occurred without weight gain or changes in calorie intake, suggesting that the nutrient-rich combination could support cardiovascular health through a simple dietary adjustment.</description>
			<pubDate>Tue, 03 Nov 2026 07:27:14 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221215.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221211.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider have uncovered compelling new evidence that even relatively small atomic collisions can recreate the extraordinary state of matter that filled the universe moments after the Big Bang. Known as quark-gluon plasma, this exotic substance forms at temperatures more than 100,000 times hotter than the center of the Sun, causing ordinary particles to break apart into their fundamental building blocks.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 21:39:04 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221211.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221209.htm</link>
			<description>NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the solar system’s origins by studying 27 tiny, distant objects beyond Neptune. Scientists discovered that these ancient building blocks of planets have remained remarkably unchanged for billions of years, while their unexpected sizes and numbers challenge existing theories of planet formation.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 22:07:01 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221209.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there’s a surprising catch</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221203.htm</link>
			<description>A massive study of nearly 486,000 adults found that regularly drinking tea was associated with an 11% lower risk of heart and blood vessel diseases. The lowest risk was linked to drinking roughly six to eight cups per day, with black tea showing more consistent benefits than green tea.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 06:29:04 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221203.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221201.htm</link>
			<description>A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmos’s deepest mysteries.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 00:33:36 EDT</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221201.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Even moderate drinking linked to cancer and early death, major study finds</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221159.htm</link>
			<description>A major new study challenges the idea that moderate drinking is safe, finding that even relatively small amounts of alcohol increase the risk of cancer, heart disease, and premature death. Researchers found no overall health benefits from drinking and warn that consuming more than one alcoholic beverage per day can significantly increase long-term health risks.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 23:12:24 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221159.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221157.htm</link>
			<description>A major new review challenges the growing enthusiasm for medical cannabis as an insomnia treatment, finding little reliable evidence that it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or daytime functioning. Researchers caution that this doesn't mean cannabis is ineffective, only that existing studies are too weak to establish whether it works.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 20:46:26 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221157.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221155.htm</link>
			<description>A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 19:34:59 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221155.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>30,000-year-old DNA reveals Ice Age Europeans were far more connected than we thought</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221153.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have uncovered surprising DNA evidence that Europeans living more than 30,000 years ago were connected across vast distances, challenging the idea that ancient populations remained largely isolated. Genetic clues from human remains and cave sediments reveal prehistoric migration, long-lasting communities, and survival through the harshest conditions of the Ice Age.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 02:30:31 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221153.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221151.htm</link>
			<description>Researchers have developed a remarkable new electronic implant that could transform type 2 diabetes treatment by lowering blood sugar without insulin or traditional drugs. The device uses a special electrically powered catalyst to convert excess glucose into a substance that the body eliminates through urine, potentially preventing unwanted energy from being stored as fat. In diabetic mice, the implant precisely controlled blood sugar and promoted weight loss.</description>
			<pubDate>Mon, 02 Nov 2026 07:47:18 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031221151.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031013035.htm</link>
			<description>A UCLA study found that long-term exposure to a common pesticide was linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease. Scientists also uncovered how the chemical damages brain cells and identified a promising way to protect them.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 07:33:13 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031013035.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031012912.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists at Johns Hopkins have uncovered a crucial missing link between a common gut bacterium and colorectal cancer, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for nearly two decades. The bacterium, Bacteroides fragilis, produces a toxin that damages the colon’s protective lining, triggers chronic inflammation, and promotes tumor formation.</description>
			<pubDate>Sat, 31 Oct 2026 09:49:23 EDT</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031012912.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031011638.htm</link>
			<description>A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 05:32:46 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261031011638.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030003022.htm</link>
			<description>A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.</description>
			<pubDate>Sat, 31 Oct 2026 09:09:49 EDT</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030003022.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030003017.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed a promising new strategy to fight glioblastoma, one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat forms of brain cancer. Their experimental approach combines focused ultrasound, tiny nanoparticles, and genetic molecules called microRNAs to attack multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 05:49:13 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030003017.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030003006.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.</description>
			<pubDate>Sat, 31 Oct 2026 22:44:28 EDT</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030003006.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists discover a hidden driver of high cholesterol and a way to stop it</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030003003.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have uncovered a hidden mechanism that allows high-cholesterol diets to undermine the body's natural cholesterol defenses, and blocking it dramatically lowered harmful LDL cholesterol in mice. Even more promising, an experimental drug targeting this pathway has already passed an early human safety trial, potentially speeding the development of a new treatment for high cholesterol.</description>
			<pubDate>Sat, 31 Oct 2026 21:57:50 EDT</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030003003.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030003001.htm</link>
			<description>A surprising new study suggests that eating peanuts every day could help support brain health and memory in older adults. Researchers found that consuming about two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions important for memory, a function that often weakens with age and has been linked to Alzheimer's disease.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 08:24:51 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030003001.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030002957.htm</link>
			<description>Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 06:45:10 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030002957.htm</guid>
		</item>
		<item>
			<title>Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030002940.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.</description>
			<pubDate>Sun, 01 Nov 2026 06:55:46 EST</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030002940.htm</guid>

			<title>Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030002935.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists have recreated a primordial state of matter from the dawn of the universe by colliding oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The surprising results show that this exotic substance can form in smaller, lower-energy collisions than previously demonstrated, challenging the known boundaries of early-universe physics.</description>
			<pubDate>Fri, 30 Oct 2026 22:09:38 EDT</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030002935.htm</guid>

		<item>
			<title>Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030002931.htm</link>
			<description>Two astronauts completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk to install a new solar array on the International Space Station, bringing NASA one step closer to a major power upgrade. Once the final array is installed on November 5, the station will have up to 30% more available power, supporting critical operations and its eventual controlled deorbit.</description>

			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030002931.htm</guid>

			<title>The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030002922.htm</link>
			<description>Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.</description>
			<pubDate>Fri, 30 Oct 2026 07:34:16 EDT</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261030002922.htm</guid>

			<title>A computer scientist breaks through a limit that stood since 1996</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261029072146.htm</link>
			<description>A computer scientist has achieved a breakthrough in a nearly 25-year-old problem involving how computers calculate distances across enormous networks. The new algorithm delivers more reliable estimates for closely connected points without sacrificing speed, overcoming a longstanding limitation of earlier methods. Its secret lies in a smarter way of sampling network connections at multiple scales.</description>

			<title>A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261029072142.htm</link>
			<description>A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzheimer’s before memory problems begin.</description>
			<pubDate>Fri, 30 Oct 2026 20:59:52 EDT</pubDate>
			<guid isPermaLink="true">https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261029072142.htm</guid>

			<title>Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice</title>
			<link>https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261029072132.htm</link>
			<description>In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.</description>
